articles.title: 'Opportunities for all': What King Harald’s speech said about integration in Norway
articles.content:
Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        As we enter the final months of the year, the government and the King have laid out their political roadmap for 2027. In the King's "Speech from the Throne", the message about immigration and integration was direct and firm.

​King Harald V gave the annual Speech from the Throne (Trontalen) on Friday, October 2nd, officially opening the 171st session of the Norwegian Parliament.

Written by the government to outline its main legislative priorities for the coming year, the speech opened with "Norway is to be a safe country with opportunities for all."

READ ALSO: What’s on the political agenda in Norway this autumn?

The address framed integration policy directly around employment, social participation, and stricter language requirements.

It linked integration to the government's goal of bringing 150,000 more people into the workforce by 2030, which marks a stricter approach to supporting and integrating newcomers.

The speech explicitly said: “People who come to Norway to settle are to be met with clearer demands and expectations as regards learning Norwegian, participating in society and finding work.”

This aligns directly with the government's commitment to the "work line" policy, emphasising that state integration programmes and social support will remain strictly tied to active efforts to learn Norwegian and find work.

By including foreign residents in Norway's plan to address labour shortages, the speech also showed a clear focus on helping newcomers join the workforce quickly instead of depending on long-term state support. This suggests that policy changes may come in the future.

Besides integration, the speech also covered other important national priorities.

The government described the current international situation as the most serious security challenge since World War II. It promised economic policies to support households and families, improve housing affordability, set clearer digital rules for young people, and reform the healthcare system.

articles.content:
Nødetater rykket til Langgangen på E18 ved Porsgrunn etter melding om trafikkulykke rundt halv åtte mandag kveld.

Situasjon skapte ifølge NRKs reporter flere kilometer med kø i begge retninger.

Trafikken var stillestående på stedet. E18 ble stengt i begge kjøreretninger fordi elgen lå i veibanen.

Ifølge politiet er det allerede redusert hastighet der påkjørselen skjedde på grunn av ombygging av E18.

Klokken 20.01 oppdaterer politiet at kjøreretning mot Larvik er åpnet, og halv ni er også kjøreretning mot Kristiansand åpnet igjen.

Fører er en mann i 80-årene som fikk tilsyn av ambulansepersonell. Elgen ble avlivet.

En elg på E18 måtte avlives og skapte full stopp i begge retninger.

articles.title: Overqualified and underpaid: The reality facing Norway's foreign workers
articles.content:
Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        Four in ten highly educated immigrants in Norway are currently employed in roles below their skill level. This mismatch takes a personal and financial toll on these workers and means Norway misses out on valuable talent.

Relocating to Norway often comes with high expectations, yet for thousands of foreign professionals, arrival marks the beginning of an uphill struggle.

A  very common story in Norway is that even with Master’s degrees and years of experience, many newcomers (or even long time residents) cannot break into their own field.

Given Norway’s high cost of living, immediate income is an absolute necessity. As a result, highly qualified individuals are forced to take up jobs in cleaning, hospitality or retail.

Stories of former lawyers with fifteen years of legal experience cleaning houses or experienced engineers delivering food are far from rare and unfortunately not anecdotal. They reflect an everyday reality for a big portion of Norway’s international workforce.

A study from Statistics Norway (SSB) shows that these personal stories are part of a bigger ongoing structural problem.

Data shows that in 2025, 93,000 immigrants with higher education in Norway worked in jobs that did not match their qualifications. This made up 40 percent of all foreign workers with higher education degrees.

This means many immigrants are employed in roles with lower educational requirements that are completely unrelated to the fields they spent years studying and specialising in.

The highest rate of overqualification is found among non-European immigrants.

Nevertheless, the official total of 93,000 understates the true scale of the issue as SSB does not count foreign workers who have lived in Norway for less than two years. If new arrivals were included, many of whom take any job at first, the total would be much higher.

In short, the 93,000 figure represents merely a baseline rather than the full scale of the issue.

READ ALSO: Foreigners in Norway face '60 percent' lower chance of promotion

While the proportion of overqualified foreign workers has remained stable at around 40 percent over the past decade, the total number of people affected has gone up significantly.

As overall immigration has increased, the total count of overqualified foreign professionals rose from 73,000 in 2021 to 93,000 in 2025.

From 2022 to 2025, the number of overqualified foreign workers grew by 23 percent, which is a bit faster than the 20 percent growth in the total foreign workforce.

This increase happened mostly because many displaced Ukrainians entered the job market quickly and many of them have higher education degrees but started out in entry-level jobs.

While national economic reports frequently highlight rising average wages and strong purchasing power in Norway, many foreign workers feel these numbers do not match their reality.

Overqualified foreign workers had a median monthly wage of 43,840 kroner, while those in jobs that matched their qualifications earned 66,150 kroner.  This means qualified foreign talent loses over 22,000 kroner every month, adding up to more than 267,000 kroner lost per year!

However, the data reveals another systemic disparity that international residents face in Norway.

Overqualified foreign workers also earn less than overqualified workers in the general population. The median monthly salary for all overqualified workers was 49,340 kroner, which is 12.5 percent more than what overqualified foreign workers make.

Foreign professionals who manage to secure relevant positions earn a 51 percent salary premium over their overqualified peers.

In the case of Ukranians in Norway, the reality is even harsher. In 2025, overqualified immigrants with a Ukrainian background had a median monthly salary of  39,210 kroner (around 26,000 kroner less each month).

Most overqualified workers get jobs in sectors that require less education and have more flexible hiring processes.

In 2025, about 31,000 overqualified immigrants worked in retail, hospitality and catering. Areas where jobs with lower wage levels are more frequent.

Approximately 21,000 overqualified immigrants worked in the health and social care industries.

On the bright side, in the Manufacturing, Construction and Energy sector, overqualification rates have steadily dropped since 2018.  Driven by Norway's growing need for technical experts, foreign engineers and specialists now find it easier to get jobs that match their qualifications.

READ MORE: Which industries employ the most workers in Norway?

Besides the financial loss, this situation is emotionally hard for foreign professionals.

Moving to Norway often means taking a big step back in their careers, losing the professional identity they worked so hard to build. Starting over and taking entry-level jobs just to get by causes frustration, anxiety and stress.

Losing professional status so quickly can also hurt self-esteem and often leads to mental health challenges in the first years after moving.

For former lawyers, architects, or teachers, working as cleaners or waiters is a tough psychological blow. It makes adjusting to a new country even harder, and many in this situation quietly wonder: What am I actually doing in Norway?

READ ALSO: What should you do if your boss or landlord in Norway is exploiting you?

On paper, employment rates among immigrants may have improved. However, this reliance on quick job placement also hides deeper economic vulnerabilities.

Many studies show that not deploying talent already in the country can be costly for national productivity and society as a whole.

Holding 93,000 academics, engineers, educators and specialists in low-skilled roles represents a major economic loss in unutilised human capital. This is especially true now, as Norwegian industries urgently need more qualified workers.

articles.title: REVEALED: What's the main reason driving foreigners to leave Norway?
articles.content:
Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        Every year, around 30,000 people pack their bags and leave Norway. While many are simply returning home, a major research project has uncovered a surprising factor driving these departures.

For many international residents, the Norwegian approach to medicine, often described by foreign residents half-jokingly as "take a paracetamol and wait," represents more than a minor inconvenience.

According to a new report published by forskning.no, the country's healthcare culture and system is indeed a contributing reason for leaving the country entirely.

These findings come from "ExitNorway," a large research project led by Aadne Aasland, a welfare and migration researcher at OsloMet.

"We were surprised when we saw this in the results," Aasland told forskning.no. "It is a tendency. We encountered dissatisfaction with health services among all groups of immigrants."

Although the healthcare system is seldom the sole reason for emigration, researchers observed that health services are more frequently cited as reasons for departure than for remaining in the country.

If you have ever felt your General Practitioner (fastlege) has blocked your request to be referred to a specialist, you are not alone. The study highlights that this is the most common complaint, among foreign leavers.

"They experience the GP as a gatekeeper who blocks the way to specialists and medications that they feel they need," Aasland explained.

In many countries, patients are used to direct access to specialists, expedited diagnostic testing, and a more proactive approach to prescribing medications. In contrast, the Norwegian system is built on strict filtering and a restrictive approach to medication, especially antibiotics.

One Ukrainian refugee interviewed for the project described the confusion: "I asked him about some tests I used to take in Ukraine. The doctor said there was no reason to send me to a specialist at this stage. But in Ukraine, it was always a specialist who checked me."

Interviews with international residents revealed that this was a widespread feeling in the community.

The frustration runs so deep that some reported travelling back to their home countries, or to places like Germany or France, for medical treatment. Others even stated they prefer the insurance-based systems of the US, simply to circumvent the Norwegian "gatekeeper" model.

Sebastian, an artist from Ecuador residing in Norway since 2019, has experienced this frustration firsthand.

He reported that he has managed a chronic condition for 18 years, requiring regular monitoring and testing. Upon relocating to Norway, it took over three years and consultations with four different General Practitioners before he found a physician willing to address his concerns.

"It was a very frustrating period, and my condition actually worsened," he shared.

He described feeling ignored and dismissed, despite bringing all his medical records from his home country to prove his treatment history. He simply could not understand why they refused to order the specific tests he needed.

"One doctor finally agreed to run tests, but they screened for something I didn't have, so it was useless," he explained.

Desperate for answers, he eventually turned to the private sector. "I had to go to a private doctor, who informed me that my condition had become severe because I hadn't had treatment or checks for so long."

"Now I have to live with a more serious condition that could have been prevented if they had just listened to me," he concluded.

The research describes this disconnect as a "culture crash."

Although the Norwegian healthcare system is intended to be egalitarian and efficient, individuals from the United States or other European countries may perceive it as dismissive or excessively slow.

"They (foreign residents) are astonished that we wait so long to seek help," Aasland said. "They themselves go to the doctor faster, even with minor things like colds."

The study also identifies a significant disparity in perception. While many foreign residents feel their concerns are not acknowledged, the local population generally expresses trust in the healthcare system.

According to the Norwegian Institute of Public Health (FHI), a large majority of Norwegians are satisfied with their GPs. In a recent health policy barometer, 81 per cent reported good experiences.

articles.title: The reasons Norway might reject your Norwegian citizenship application
articles.content:
Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        Norwegian citizenship comes with a hefty application fee and plenty of requirements. There are several reasons why the Norwegian Directorate of Immigration might reject an application.

Lifetime enrollment in the Norwegian National Insurance Scheme, the ability to live in Norway for as long as you wish, and returning to Norway after a few years away without going through the immigration process are some of the many benefits of Norwegian citizenship.

Norwegian citizenship doesn’t come easy, though. In addition to waiting years to become eligible, you will have to pass language and citizenship tests, provide a criminal record certificate, verify your identity and meet the requirements for permanent residence if you don’t hold it already.

This is all before you pay 6,500 kroner to apply for Norwegian citizenship.

So, what are the reasons why the Norwegian Directorate of Immigration (UDI) turns down applications?

This applies not just to your citizenship application but also to your entire stay. If you bend the rules when it comes to the residence requirements, you could find your citizenship application rejected.

Even if your application is successful, you will find your citizenship revoked later if the UDI finds out. The UDI will still revoke your citizenship, even if you are the one who decides to come clean to them.

Should the authorities have reason to believe that you have provided incorrect information on any residence or citizenship applications, they will typically invite you for an interview with the police or notify you of your revocation in advance.

READ MORE: How Norway can revoke residency and citizenship over wrong details

This one might seem obvious, but it can happen relatively easily. One of the most common reasons for a foreign national having their citizenship rejected is not passing the citizenship or social studies test (in Norwegian).

For the citizenship test, you must answer 24 out of 36 multiple-choice questions correctly.

The social studies test is taken by those who typically have been through the social studies course for immigrants.

Language-wise, you will generally have to have passed an oral test in Norwegian at  B1 level.

Another common pitfall is the criminal record certificate. Criminal record certificates are only valid for three months. The certification proves that you haven’t been convicted of any crimes and are not disqualified from applying for citizenship.

As the certificate can only be valid for three months, the UDI advises that you shouldn’t order the certificate until you have an appointment to hand in your documents to the police. This reduces the likelihood of the certificate expiring before your documents are handed in.

Failure to meet any of the citizenship requirements will result in your application being turned down. You must also hold a valid residence permit whilst applying for citizenship.

Remember that under standard rules, you must have stayed in Norway for a total of eight of the past eleven years and held residence permits that were each valid for at least one year.

On the UDI website, you can learn how to calculate residence periods in exception cases. However, as there is currently a proposal to amend the Citizenship Act, which could alter how qualifying residence time is measured, these requirements may change in the future.

READ MORE: What will Norway's plan to toughen citizenship rules mean for you?

Being convicted of a criminal offence that results in a fine or prison sentence will bar you from being eligible for citizenship for a set period of time.

The disqualification period can range from 2.5 years up to 39 years, depending on the severity of your punishment. You can see an overview of the disqualification rules on the UDI website.

Those who have received fixed penalty notices rather than criminal fines will not be disqualified. Those who have had charges or cases dropped are also not disqualified.

An example of a fixed penalty notice would be a fine for minor or moderate speeding.

To be eligible for citizenship, you also need to be eligible for permanent residence at the same time, which can make matters confusing.

For many, the easiest way around this is to just hold permanent residence as proof of eligibility while applying for citizenship.

The key thing to look out for when it comes to citizenship is the minimum income requirements for non-EEA permanent residence applicants.

One of the requirements for permanent residence applications for non-EEA nationals is that you will need to have fulfilled the income requirements for the previous 12 months and that you cannot have received financial assistance (økonomisk sosialhjelp) during the prior 12 months.

articles.content:
Et israelsk luftangrep drepte minst fem palestinere i en leilighetsbygning i Gaza by natt til lørdag, ifølge helsemyndighetene i området, melder Reuters.

Det israelske militæret har ikke kommentert hendelsen.

Etter at USA fremforhandlet en våpenhvile på Gazastripen i fjor, har partene vært uenige om vilkårene for at Hamas skal avvæpnes og at Israel skal trekke seg ut.

Israel, som hevder Hamas har rustet opp igjen og gjennomført angrep i strid med våpenhvilen, har trappet opp angrepene mot gruppen de siste ukene.

Hamas avviser anklagene og hevder Israel undergraver våpenhvilen.

Krigen i Gaza

Konflikten mellom Israel og Hamas eskalerte etter angrepet fra Hamas 7. oktober 2023. Siden har Israel ført krig mot Gaza, hvor Hamas regjerer. Over 65.000 palestinere er drept, og FN har slått alarm om katastrofal sult i Gaza.

articles.content:

Sør-Korea har over 50 millioner innbyggere og er et av Asias tettest befolkede land. Yoon Suk-yeol fra Det konservative partiet er landets avsatte president. Tirsdag 3. desember erklærte han militær unntakstilstand.

articles.title: Did you know that Oslo has its own Mona Lisa?
articles.content:
Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        Whether you're an art lover visiting Oslo or a local looking for something different to do, the Norwegian capital holds a rather fun surprise for you.

Yes, you read that correctly: the Mona Lisa and Norway in the same sentence.

The Nasjonalmuseet (Oslo’s National Museum) has its own 17th-century version of the Mona Lisa.

Painted by an unknown artist, this intriguing replica is currently on display in Room 061 as part of the 'Moods and emotions' exhibition.

With autumn here and rainy days ahead, it’s a great time to pop in and catch a glimpse of Leonardo da Vinci's famous masterpiece (or at least a historic copy of it) and see that mysterious smile up close, right in the centre of Oslo.

You are sure to find it much less crowded than in Paris.

The National Museum is Norway’s largest collection of art, architecture and design. If you fancy a visit, you can find the museum’s opening hours here.

articles.content:

Det er en historisk dag når kong Haakon fredag gjør en av sine viktigste oppgaver som konge. Dronning Mette-Marit kan ikke delta grunnet sykdom.

Stortinget

Riksrevisjonen har undersøkt 500 stortingsrepresentanters bruk av blant annet pendlerboliger, reiseutgifter og etterlønn. Over 60 har fått for mye utbetalt og kontrollen har vært for dårlig, konkluderer riksrevisoren.

articles.title: Nytt angrep på tankskip i Hormuzstredet
articles.content:
Et tankskip begynte å brenne etter å ha blitt truffet av et prosjektil i Hormuzstredet, opplyser britiske UKMTO.

Skipsovervåkingstjenesten fikk melding fra en tredjepart om at skipet ble truffet av et ukjent prosjektil mens det var på vei gjennom det viktige stredet.

Brannen om bord ble raskt slukket, og mannskapet skal være i sikkerhet.

Det er ikke avklart hvor store skader skipet fikk eller om angrepet har ført til miljøødeleggelser. Myndighetene etterforsker saken, men det er foreløpig ikke klart hvem som skjøt mot skipet.

Iran blokkerer fortsatt det meste av trafikken gjennom Hormuzstredet, som forbinder Persiabukta med Indiahavet. I fredstid passerer rundt en femdel av verdens olje gjennom det strategisk viktige farvannet. (NTB)

Iran

Iran er en islamsk republikk i Midtøsten. Siden 28. februar har landet vært i krig med USA og Israel. Samtidig har det siden slutten av 2025 vært store demonstrasjoner mot det ultrakonservative, undertrykkende regimet i landet.
